summary.text: Letting \(m=D(n)\), the congruence \(n\equiv m\pmod 9\) gives \(n=m+9r\), while a pigeonhole argument makes the powers \(10^e\bmod m\) eventually periodic. A multiset of \(n\) exponents whose powers sum to \(m10^{M+r}\) is spread apart by this period to make them distinct; thus their power-sum \(k\) is divisible by \(m\), has exactly \(n\) decimal ones and hence \(D(k)=n\), and choosing all exponents at least \(n\) ensures \(k>n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(r)
\]
denote the sum of the decimal digits of the nonnegative integer \(r\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a distinct positive integer \(K\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid K\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(K)\mid n.
\]
This will show that the set of Harshad amicable partners of \(n\) is nonempty. Its least member is then positive, so the sequence value \(a(n)\), defined to be that least member when the set is nonempty and to be \(0\) otherwise, cannot be zero.

We first record several elementary facts that will be used in the construction.

### 1. Elementary facts about decimal digits

For every positive integer \(r\), one has \(D(r)>0\). Indeed, if the sum of the decimal digits were zero, then every digit, being nonnegative, would be zero. Reconstructing the number from its decimal digits would then give \(r=0\), a contradiction.

Also,
\[
D(r)\le r.
\]
To see this directly, write the decimal digits from least significant to most significant as \(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_t\). Then
\[
r=\sum_{j=0}^t d_j10^j,
\qquad
D(r)=\sum_{j=0}^t d_j.
\]
Since \(10^j\ge 1\) for every \(j\), the second sum is at most the first.

Furthermore,
\[
r\equiv D(r)\pmod 9.
\]
This follows from \(10\equiv1\pmod9\), and hence \(10^j\equiv1\pmod9\) for every \(j\):
\[
r=\sum_j d_j10^j\equiv\sum_jd_j=D(r)\pmod9.
\]

Finally, for every \(r\ge0\),
\[
r<10^r.
\]
This can be proved by induction. It is true for \(r=0\), since \(0<1\). If \(r<10^r\), then
\[
r+1\le 10^r+1<10^r+9\cdot10^r=10^{r+1},
\]
because \(10^r\ge1\).

### 2. Eventual periodicity of powers of ten modulo an arbitrary positive modulus

Let \(m>0\). There exist integers \(M_0\ge0\) and \(P>0\) such that
\[
10^{x+P}\equiv10^x\pmod m
\qquad\text{for every }x\ge M_0.
\]

Indeed, consider the \(m+1\) residues
\[
10^0,10^1,\ldots,10^m\pmod m.
\]
There are only \(m\) residue classes modulo \(m\), so two of these powers have the same residue. Choose \(0\le i<j\le m\) with
\[
10^i\equiv10^j\pmod m.
\]
Set
\[
M_0=i,
\qquad
P=j-i>0.
\]
For any \(x\ge i\), write \(x=i+d\). Multiplying the displayed congruence by \(10^d\) gives
\[
10^x=10^{i+d}\equiv10^{j+d}=10^{x+P}\pmod m.
\]

By iterating this congruence, for every \(y\ge M_0\) and every integer \(s\ge0\),
\[
10^{y+sP}\equiv10^y\pmod m. \tag{1}
\]
This follows by induction on \(s\), applying the one-period congruence at the exponent \(y+sP\), which is still at least \(M_0\).

### 3. Decomposing \(n\) using its digit sum

Fix a positive integer \(n\), and put
\[
m=D(n).
\]
By the first digit fact, \(m>0\). The modulo-nine identity gives
\[
n\equiv m\pmod9,
\]
and the inequality \(D(n)\le n\) gives \(m\le n\). Consequently \(n-m\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(9\). Thus there is an integer \(q\ge0\) such that
\[
n=m+9q. \tag{2}
\]

Apply the eventual-periodicity result with this positive modulus \(m\), obtaining \(M_0\) and \(P>0\). Define
\[
M=\max(M_0,n).
\]
Thus every exponent at least \(M\) lies in the periodic range, and also \(M\ge n\).

### 4. A nondecreasing list of base exponents

We now form a list \(B\) of integers as follows:

* first include one copy of \(M\);
* for each \(r=0,1,\ldots,q-1\), include nine copies of \(M+r\);
* finally include \(m-1\) copies of \(M+q\).

If \(q=0\), the middle portion is empty. The list is in nondecreasing order, and every one of its entries is at least \(M\).

Its length is
\[
1+9q+(m-1)=m+9q=n \tag{3}
\]
by (2). Write its entries, in order, as
\[
y_0,y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}.
\]

The sum of the corresponding powers of ten has a particularly simple form. The middle portion contributes
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{q-1}9\cdot10^{M+r}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{q-1}\bigl(10^{M+r+1}-10^{M+r}\bigr)
 =10^{M+q}-10^M.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}10^{y_i}
&=10^M+\bigl(10^{M+q}-10^M\bigr)+(m-1)10^{M+q}\\
&=m10^{M+q}. \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, this sum is divisible by \(m\).

### 5. Separating all exponents while preserving the sum modulo \(m\)

The list \(B\) may contain repeated exponents. To turn its power sum into a decimal number having only zeroes and ones as digits, we separate the exponents using the period \(P\). For \(0\le i<n\), define
\[
e_i=y_i+iP.
\]

These exponents are strictly increasing. In fact, if \(i<j\), then \(y_i\le y_j\), because the list \(B\) is nondecreasing, and
\[
e_j-e_i=(y_j-y_i)+(j-i)P>0
\]
since \(P>0\). Thus all \(e_i\) are distinct.

Moreover, every \(y_i\ge M\ge M_0\). Applying (1) with \(s=i\) gives
\[
10^{e_i}=10^{y_i+iP}\equiv10^{y_i}\pmod m.
\]
Summing these congruences and using (4), we obtain
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}10^{e_i}
\equiv \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}10^{y_i}
=m10^{M+q}
\equiv0\pmod m. \tag{5}
\]

Define
\[
K=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}10^{e_i}. \tag{6}
\]
Equation (5) says precisely that
\[
m=D(n)\mid K. \tag{7}
\]

### 6. The decimal digit sum of \(K\)

Because the exponents \(e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1}\) are distinct, the sum (6) has no carrying in base ten. More explicitly, let \(E=1+\max_i e_i\), and define decimal digits \(c_0,\ldots,c_{E-1}\) by
\[
c_j=
\begin{cases}
1,&j\in\{e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1}\},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then every \(c_j<10\), and
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{E-1}c_j10^j
 =\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}10^{e_i}
 =K.
\]
Thus these are exactly the decimal digits of \(K\). Since there is one digit equal to \(1\) for each of the \(n\) distinct exponents and all remaining digits are zero,
\[
D(K)=\sum_{j=0}^{E-1}c_j=n. \tag{8}
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
D(K)=n\mid n. \tag{9}
\]

### 7. Positivity and distinctness

There are exactly \(n\) exponents in the construction, and \(n>0\), so the sum defining \(K\) is nonempty and hence positive.

We also show that \(K\ne n\), in fact \(K>n\). Every base exponent \(y_i\) is at least \(M\), so every shifted exponent satisfies
\[
e_i=y_i+iP\ge M\ge n.
\]
Choose any one of the exponents, which is possible because \(n>0\). Then
\[
K\ge10^{e_i}\ge10^n>n,
\]
where the final inequality was proved in Section 1. Therefore \(K>0\) and \(K\ne n\).

Combining (7), (8), and the preceding paragraph, \(K\) satisfies
\[
K>0,
\qquad K\ne n,
\qquad D(n)\mid K,
\qquad D(K)\mid n.
\]
Hence \(K\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\).

Since \(n>0\) was arbitrary, every positive integer has at least one such partner. For each fixed positive \(n\), the set
\[
\{k\in\mathbb N:k>0,\ k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is therefore nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least member, and that least member is positive because every member of the set is positive. By definition this least member is \(a(n)\). Consequently
\[
a(n)\ne0
\]
for every positive integer \(n\), as claimed.
